passage: Nirmala, you said you can't do spreadsheet formulas. Let me tell you about me at twenty-five, at the post office in Amritsar, the year the computers came. Everyone younger learned fast. I sat there resenting the machine, saying, "I can't do this. I'm not a computer person." One evening the postmaster, an old Sikh gentleman, heard me and said, "Gurpreet, you can't do it yet. What will you try next?" That word annoyed me, honestly. But I went home and wrote on a paper: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day." It wasn't magic. My first method, copying from the manual, didn't help at all. Harjit's way did. So, Nirmala: yet, and then, what will you try?

qa.q: What did young Gurpreet write on the paper at home?
qa.a: "Can't do it YET. Next: ask Harjit to show me the entry screen, practise ten entries a day."

qa.q: Why did the word "yet" annoy young Gurpreet at first?
qa.a: Gurpreet was full of resentment toward the machine and felt stuck; "yet" sounded too easy, as if it brushed aside how hard it felt.

qa.q: Which choice made "yet" actually work for Gurpreet?
qa.a: Pairing it with a concrete next step, and switching from the manual to Harjit's way when the first method failed.

qa.q: What might Nirmala take from this story?
qa.a: Nirmala may see that struggling with formulas now doesn't close the future, and that the useful question is what to try next.

grounding: An elder recalls turning 'I can't' into 'I can't yet' at twenty-five and pairing it with a better strategy.

passage: Maria had failed her driving test in Panaji twice, both times on the slope start, and her new job at a clinic in Mapusa needed her driving in three weeks. The monsoon had turned the practice ground to mud. After the second fail she sat in Simran's car in the rain and said, "I can't do this. I'm just not a driver." Simran didn't argue. "You can't do slope starts yet. What haven't you tried?" Maria wiped her eyes, annoyed. Then she thought. She had only ever practised on flat roads. She'd never used the handbrake method the instructor mentioned. The next morning, rain still falling, she found a quiet sloping lane near the church and did twenty slope starts with the handbrake. Nineteen didn't roll back.

qa.q: How many of Maria's slope starts didn't roll back?
qa.a: Nineteen of twenty.

qa.q: Why was Maria annoyed when Simran said "yet"?
qa.a: After two fails and with a deadline looming, she felt defeated, and "yet" seemed to brush past how bad she felt.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Simran's question about what she hadn't tried; Maria chose to practise on a real slope with the handbrake method instead of flat roads.

qa.q: How might Simran feel seeing Maria practise in the rain?
qa.a: Simran may feel glad that a short question helped, and quietly proud of a friend who turned tears into a plan.

grounding: An adult under time pressure reframes 'I can't drive' as 'not yet' and finds a better practice strategy.

passage: At the Nariman Point office, Hrithik's first client presentation had gone badly: he lost his place, read from the slides, and watched the client check his phone. Back at his desk he muttered, "I can't present. Some people just can't." Pankaj, the senior manager, overheard. "You can't present yet," Pankaj said. "So what's the next thing to try?" Hrithik almost rolled his eyes; it sounded like a poster. But that night he wrote two lines: "Can't present yet. Try: practise out loud three times, use cue cards not slides." He rehearsed in the empty conference room, twice to the wall and once to Pankaj. The next presentation wasn't perfect. But he didn't read from the slides, and the client asked two questions.

qa.q: What did Hrithik decide to use instead of reading from the slides?
qa.a: Cue cards.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik almost roll his eyes at Pankaj's "yet"?
qa.a: Still stinging from the bad presentation, he felt it was a slogan that ignored how badly things had gone.

qa.q: Which choice turned "yet" into progress?
qa.a: Writing a concrete plan, practising aloud and using cue cards, so the word led to a better strategy rather than just hope.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Hrithik's second presentation?
qa.a: Pankaj would likely see real progress, fewer slides read aloud and a client asking questions, and feel the nudge was worth it.

grounding: An adult reframes a failed presentation with 'not yet' and a specific practice plan, and improves.

passage:
"I can't do it, Saurabh. I'm quitting the swimming class."
Her husband looked up from the laptop. "What happened?"
"Everyone else floated by week three. I still sink like a stone. I'm twenty-five, I'm too old, I just can't swim."
"Can't, or can't yet?"
Sonali threw a wet towel at him. "Don't do the poster thing."
"I'm not. Just... what have you tried?"
She sat down, dripping. "Kicking harder. It makes it worse."
"So kicking harder isn't it. What else is there?"
A pause. "The coach said something about breathing out slowly and keeping my head down. I kept lifting it to look."
"So try that on Saturday?"
"Fine." She wrung out her hair. "I can't float. Yet." She said the last word as if she didn't quite trust it. "And I'll ask the coach to watch my head."

qa.q: What did the coach say about breathing and her head?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly and keeping her head down.

qa.q: What is Sonali feeling when she says 'Yet' as if she doesn't quite trust it?
qa.a: Still frustrated and doubtful, but opening a door; she half-believes progress is possible and is willing to test it.

qa.q: What turning point in the conversation helped Sonali plan her next try?
qa.a: Saurabh asking what she had tried; seeing that kicking harder made it worse led her to a new strategy, breathing out and head down, with the coach watching.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel when the towel comes flying?
qa.a: Saurabh probably takes it with good humour 😄, understands her frustration, and chooses questions over slogans so she doesn't feel lectured.

grounding: An adult turns 'I can't swim' into 'I can't yet' and pairs it with a new strategy to try next.

passage: When I moved to Bengaluru for my first nursing job, I told everyone, "I can't speak Kannada. I'm hopeless with languages." I'm Beena, from Kottayam. For three months I pointed and smiled at patients' families and felt useless. My friend Kiranjit, a Punjabi who'd learned Tamil in Chennai, said, "You mean you can't yet." I rolled my eyes. But the word stuck. Then she asked, "What have you actually tried?" Honestly, just a phrasebook I never opened. So I changed the plan: five ward phrases a week, written on my palm, used with real patients, and the night-shift attendant correcting me. Four months later I can explain the meal times and ask where it hurts. Plenty still goes over my head. But "I can't" has become "not yet, and here are next week's five."

qa.q: How many ward phrases did Beena learn each week?
qa.a: Five ward phrases a week.

qa.q: Why did Beena feel useless in the first three months?
qa.a: Without Kannada, Beena could only point and smile instead of really helping families, and 'I'm hopeless with languages' made the gap feel permanent.

qa.q: What choice turned 'yet' into real progress for Beena?
qa.a: Swapping the unopened phrasebook for five phrases a week, used on the ward and corrected by the night-shift attendant; the word opened the door and the method did the work.

qa.q: How might patients' families experience the change in Beena?
qa.a: They can now hear the meal times and be asked where it hurts in their own language, which likely makes them feel more cared for and less anxious.

grounding: An adult replaces 'I can't speak the language' with 'not yet' and backs it with a concrete weekly method.

passage:
Trainee review note, week three

Siddharth joined the analytics team from a sales background. On Tuesday I gave him his first spreadsheet automation task. After an hour he came to my desk, red in the face, and said, "I can't do macros. I'm not a coding person." He sounded resentful, as if the task was unfair.

I asked him to change one word: "I can't do macros yet." He rolled his eyes but repeated it. Then I asked, "So what would you try next?" He thought and said he'd been copying code from forums without understanding it. We agreed a different strategy: record a simple macro, then read the code it produced, line by line.

By Friday he had automated the weekly report. He said, half laughing, "Still yet, for the hard ones." Next step: I'll pair him with Ravina for the database module.

— Sahil

qa.q: What did Siddharth say when he came to Sahil's desk?
qa.a: "I can't do macros. I'm not a coding person."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when he first said he couldn't do macros?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and resentful, red in the face, as if the task was unfair and proved he wasn't suited to it.

qa.q: Why did adding 'yet' help only when paired with a new strategy?
qa.a: 'Yet' kept the door open, but it was the change from copying forum code to recording and reading macros that actually gave him progress.

qa.q: What would change if Sahil had only said 'just keep trying'?
qa.a: Siddharth might have kept copying code without understanding and stayed stuck, feeling even more that he wasn't a coding person.

grounding: It shows, through a supervisor's note, an adult who changes 'I can't' to 'I can't yet' and asks what to try next, with a better strategy making the difference.

passage:
Saturday

Failed the driving test again. Second time. The examiner marked me down for reverse parking, and I honestly felt like shouting at him. It was a tiny gap. Nobody could fit in that gap.

Came home and told Ritu didi, who taught me most of what I know. I said, "I just can't drive. Some people can't." She said, "Deepak, you can't reverse park yet. You can drive fine." That annoyed me even more. But then she asked what I'd been doing to practise. The truth is, I'd been driving around the colony, which I'm already good at. Never parking.

So what to try next? Ritu didi says there's an empty ground behind the temple on Sunday mornings. We'll put out two buckets and I'll reverse between them till I'm bored.

I still think that examiner was harsh. But okay. Yet.

— Deepak

qa.q: What did the examiner mark Deepak down for?
qa.a: Reverse parking.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel after failing the test?
qa.a: Deepak felt angry and resentful toward the examiner, and discouraged enough to say some people can't drive.

qa.q: What next step did Deepak and Ritu didi choose, and why is it a better strategy?
qa.a: Practising reverse parking between two buckets on an empty ground targets the exact weak skill, instead of more easy colony driving.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi see Deepak's 'I just can't drive'?
qa.a: Ritu didi probably sees it as frustration talking, since she knows Deepak drives fine and only needs practice at parking.

grounding: It shows an adult who shifts from 'I can't drive' to 'I can't reverse park yet' and plans a new strategy for what to try next.

passage:
Ankita had been teaching at the village school in Kherwadi for three weeks, and Class 4 still ignored her. They talked over her, threw chalk, and went quiet only for Usha Ma'am, who had taught there for twenty years.
One evening, walking home past the sugarcane fields, Ankita said, “I can't manage a class. I'm just not a teacher.”
Usha Ma'am laughed. “You can't manage it yet. That's all.”
Ankita felt a flash of resentment. Easy for her to say.
But the word stayed. Yet. The next morning she tried something new: she asked Usha Ma'am what exactly she did. Usha showed her a clapping rhythm to get attention and a way to give every restless boy a job.
Ankita tried it. Half the class clapped back. Half.
“Not yet all of them,” she told herself, and planned what to try next.

qa.q: How long had Ankita been teaching at the Kherwadi school?
qa.a: She had been teaching there for three weeks.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when Usha Ma'am said “yet”?
qa.a: She felt a flash of resentment, as if it were easy advice, but the word stayed with her.

qa.q: Why did “yet” work better when Ankita paired it with asking what to try?
qa.a: “Yet” kept the future open, and asking Usha Ma'am for specific methods gave Ankita a better strategy, not just more effort.

qa.q: How might Usha Ma'am see Ankita's struggles?
qa.a: Usha Ma'am probably sees them as normal for a new teacher and feels patient and encouraging.

grounding: The passage shows an adult replacing “I can't” with “I can't yet” and asking what to try next, pairing the word with better strategy.

passage:
Abebe had moved from accounting to a data team in Addis Ababa, and the coding was brutal. By the second month, his colleague Jana watched him slam his laptop shut. “I can't do this. I'm not a programmer.”
Jana pulled up a chair. “Say it with ‘yet’ on the end.”
He rolled his eyes. “That's a poster slogan.”
“Maybe. Say it anyway.”
“I can't do this… yet.”
“Good. Now what's the next thing to try?”
He thought. “I keep copying code I don't understand. Maybe I should write smaller pieces and test them.”
“That's a strategy. The ‘yet’ isn't magic. It just gives you room to find one.”
The next week Abebe wrote tiny functions, one at a time. His bugs dropped by half. He still said “yet” out loud sometimes, a little embarrassed, but it helped.

qa.q: What did Abebe keep doing with code he didn't understand?
qa.a: He kept copying code he didn't understand.

qa.q: How did Abebe feel when Jana suggested adding “yet”?
qa.a: He felt sceptical and a bit irritated, calling it a poster slogan.

qa.q: What made “yet” useful for Abebe rather than empty?
qa.a: It was paired with a real strategy, writing and testing small pieces, so the effort had a better method behind it.

qa.q: How does Jana see Abebe's struggle?
qa.a: Jana sees it as a normal stage of learning and feels patient, helping him turn frustration into a next step.

The bank's training centre in Pune smelled of new carpet and nervous people. Imran, twenty-four, had failed the spreadsheet module test twice. The third attempt was on Friday.
“I just can't do formulas,” he muttered during the break.
Manoj, the trainer, overheard. “You can't do them yet.”
Imran felt a spike of resentment. Easy for the trainer to say.
Manoj sat down beside him. “What did you try last time?”
“I watched the videos again.”
“And?”
“Same result.”
“So more of the same effort won't help. What else could you try?”
Imran thought. “Practise with real branch data instead of the examples? Ask you when I'm stuck instead of guessing?”
“Both good.”
On Friday Imran scored 68, just over the pass mark. He wrote “yet” in the corner of his notebook, and underneath it: “new method.”

passage:
Dear Tarun,
You asked how the presenting is going. Honestly? Last month, after my first client pitch, I sat in the washroom and told myself, "I can't do this. Some people just can't speak in front of others."
Then I remembered what you used to say when we were learning to code: "Not yet." So I tried it. I can't present well yet. It sounded silly, but it changed the question from "what's wrong with me" to "what do I try next."
And the answer wasn't just "practise more." I'd practised plenty, reading my slides out loud to the wall. So I changed the method. I recorded myself on the phone, cut my slides from twenty to eight, and asked Meenal from the next team to throw hard questions at me.
Yesterday's pitch wasn't perfect. But I didn't hide in the washroom after.
Write back soon,
Rafiq

qa.a: Rafiq cut the slides from twenty to eight.

"You want the swimming story, Kavitha? Fine. I'm Tarun, I'm twenty-five, and until last year I couldn't swim at all.
The first class, I stood in the shallow end with eight-year-olds, and I swallowed half the pool. I went home and said, 'I can't swim. I never will. It's too late for me.'
My sister said, 'You can't swim yet.' I rolled my eyes. But the word stuck. It made me ask a different question. Not 'why am I useless' but 'what do I try next?'
And trying harder didn't work. I thrashed for three weeks and got nowhere. So I changed things. I asked the coach for one-to-one sessions. I practised floating only, for a whole week, before any strokes.
In March I swam one full length. Badly. But one full length.
So now when something feels impossible, I say 'yet,' and then I ask what to change."

qa.a: Tarun felt hopeless and embarrassed, believing it was too late to learn after swallowing half the pool among eight-year-olds.

qa.q: What did Tarun learn about "yet" and effort?
qa.a: "Yet" opened the question of what to try next, but thrashing harder did not help; changing the method, with one-to-one sessions and floating first, is what worked.

qa.q: How might Tarun's sister feel hearing about the full length?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and pleased that her small word helped Tarun keep going.

I share a flat with Ritu, and last month I watched her fight with bread.
She wanted to bake a proper loaf. The first one came out like a brick. She said, "I can't bake. I'm not a baking person," and nearly threw the flour away.
The next morning there was a sticky note on the fridge in her handwriting: I can't make bread YET. Below it, a list. Water too cold? Didn't knead long enough? Oven not hot enough?
I don't know what went on in her head. But she changed one thing each time. Warmer water. Longer kneading, with a timer. An oven thermometer she borrowed from me.
Loaf four was edible. Loaf six was actually good, and she gave me the heel with butter. The sticky note is still on the fridge. Someone, I think Ritu, has crossed out YET.

qa.q: Why did Ritu's approach work better than just baking again and again?
qa.a: She changed one thing at a time, water, kneading and oven heat, so her effort was guided by a strategy and each loaf taught her something.

passage:
Tuesday. Kunal's query crashed for the fourth time, and the error message might as well have been in Latin. Across the desk, Sonali finished her report in twenty minutes. "I can't do SQL," he muttered, and felt a hot little flash of resentment when she offered to look.
Thursday. He typed the same sentence into his notes, stopped, and added one word: "I can't do joins yet." Then, under it: "What do I try next?" He had spent two evenings rereading the same tutorial. That clearly wasn't working. So he asked Sonali for the smallest broken example she could think of.
The following Monday. Kunal wrote a join on a table of five rows, then fifty, then the real one. It ran. He still needed Sonali's help with the date filter, but this time he asked without the heat in his chest.
